name: The Catalpa of the Van Abbemuseum
age_estimate: around a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.neighbourhood: Eindhoven city centre, on the Dommel beside the Van Abbemuseum

access: Free. Public green strip (plantsoen) beside the museum's main entrance, open at all times.
transport: Eindhoven Centraal, about 15 minutes on foot south along the Dommel, or bus to the Van Abbemuseum stop.
verify_notes: Two independent sources: the national LRMB register (nr 1690225, planted_band 1900-1910, reason 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=ja) and the Gemeente Eindhoven open-data 'bomen' dataset (boomnummer 35956, Catalpa bignonioides, status_ter_indicatie 'Monumentaal', plantjaar 1930, hoogte 15-18m), matched at 16m from the register point, current as of the dataset's 2026-09-07 refresh (good 'alive now' evidence). AGE CONFLICT: register implies planted 1900-1910 (about 116-126 years old today), municipal record says planted 1930 (about 96 years old); no winner picked, both reported. The Van Abbemuseum (Bilderdijklaan 10) was built 1936 for cigar manufacturer Henri van Abbe's art collection, architect A.J. Kropholler; if the earlier planting date is right the tree predates the museum building, a nice detail but not stated as fact given the conflict. The same municipal dataset shows four more Catalpa bignonioides within 35m all marked 'Monumentaal', planted 1930, forming a small grove near the museum entrance; this one is the closest match to the register point (16m) and is the one to feature, though the writer could mention the grove as context. No girth or diameter figure found in either source.

name: The Cedar of Pastoor Sickingstraat
access: Free. Stands in a paved urban street setting, visible from the public street at all times.
transport: About 1.7 km southeast of Eindhoven Centraal (Joriskwartier, Stratum); bus lines serve nearby Aalsterweg, or about 20 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely on location (2.8m apart): the national LRMB register (nr 1692946, reason 'potentieel', history 'onbekend', owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=ja, no age given) and the Gemeente Eindhoven open-data 'bomen' dataset (status_ter_indicatie 'Monumentaal', plantjaar 1930, hoogte 15-18m), current as of the dataset's 2026-09-07 refresh (good 'alive now' evidence). SPECIES FLAG: the municipal dataset's own Dutch common-name field calls it 'Blauwe atlasceder' (Blue Atlas Cedar, which is normally Cedrus atlantica 'Glauca'), while its species code field and the LRMB register both say Cedrus libani (Cedar of Lebanon). Atlas cedar and Lebanon cedar are easily confused evergreen conifers with a similar blue-green habit; this looks like a mismatched label in one of the two systems rather than two different trees, since both sources point at the same coordinate. The page should ask the reader to confirm which cedar it is (needle arrangement/cone shape settle it). The Joriskwartier around it was built mostly around 2006, so this cedar is a considerably older remnant, now standing 'completely surrounded by paving' according to search-snippet-only descriptions I could not verify by viewing the source page directly (monumentaltrees.com 403s automated fetches; not used as a source, noted here only as a lead for a future viewing pass). No girth or diameter figure found in either source.

name: The Honey Locust of the Stadspaviljoen
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan 1, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely on location (3.7m apart): the national LRMB register (nr 1690253, planted_band 1890-1900, reason 'dendrologisch', owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=nee) and the Gemeente Eindhoven open-data 'bomen' dataset (status_ter_indicatie 'Monumentaal', plantjaar 1940, hoogte '>24 m'), current as of the dataset's 2026-09-07 refresh (good 'alive now' evidence). AGE CONFLICT: register implies planted 1890-1900 (about 126-136 years old today), municipal record says planted 1940 (about 86 years old); no winner picked, both reported, though either way this is a genuinely old, over-24-metre specimen. The Stadswandelpark grew out of the 19th-century Landgoed Den Elzent estate (tobacco manufacturer H.F.C. Coolen, sold 1876 to Amsterdam merchant B.H.A. Sinkel, who had Leonard Springer lay out a landscape garden); the Stadspaviljoen behind which this tree stands was the estate's former coach house, later a music kiosk, and the grounds became a public park in 1921, formally named Stadswandelpark in 1931. The municipal dataset shows this whole corner of the park is a genuine grove of 1910/1940-dated 'Monumentaal' trees (beeches, pin oaks, black locusts, a sweet chestnut) from the same historic planting phases, good context for the story. No girth or diameter figure found in either source; the >24m height is the one hard number to use instead.

name: The Sweet Chestnut of the Stadspaviljoen
age_estimate: about a century old (sources disagree on the decade)

location.address: Alberdingk Thijmlaan, Stadswandelpark, behind the Stadspaviljoen, Eindhoven

transport: About 1.3 km south of Eindhoven Centraal, inside the Stadswandelpark; several bus lines serve the park's edges, or about 15-20 minutes on foot.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree almost exactly on location (0.8m apart, effectively the same tree): the national LRMB register (nr 1690254, planted_band 1890-1900, reason 'dendrologisch', owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=nee) and the Gemeente Eindhoven open-data 'bomen' dataset (species Castanea sativa, status_ter_indicatie 'Monumentaal', plantjaar 1940, hoogte 15-18m), current as of the dataset's 2026-09-07 refresh (good 'alive now' evidence). AGE CONFLICT: register implies planted 1890-1900 (about 126-136 years old today), municipal record says 1940 (about 86 years old); no winner picked, both reported. Same park and planting history as ein_014 (the Honey Locust a few dozen metres away): the Stadswandelpark grew from the 19th-century Landgoed Den Elzent estate, became a public park in 1921 and was formally named in 1931; this corner behind the former coach house (now the Stadspaviljoen) carries a cluster of other 'Monumentaal'-rated trees from the same 1910/1940 planting phases (beeches, pin oaks, black locusts), good context for the story, and this chestnut plus the honey locust could be described as two stops on the same short walk. No girth or diameter figure found in either source. Sweet chestnuts are edible-fruiting trees; if it still produces chestnuts that could be a seasonal (best_time, autumn) detail for the writer to check on a future visit, though this pass found no direct evidence of fruiting either way.
